title: Will Putin achieve by guile what Stalin achieved with millions of troops?
summary: When a trilateral meeting between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was announced, commentators with an eye for history were soon asking whether this Shenzhen summit was going to be a second Yalta allowing Vladimir Putin to advance his revisionist agenda, writes John Herbst. The post Will Putin achieve by guile what Stalin achieved with millions of troops? appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council commentary asks whether a planned China-US-Russia summit in Shenzhen could let Putin advance his revisionist agenda.

brief.summary: The authors, led by John Herbst, argue that Putin is pursuing through influence and information operations what Stalin achieved with mass armies. They say Russia has struggled militarily in Ukraine: it failed to take Kyiv, lost ground to a Ukrainian counteroffensive, has not captured all of Donbas, and faces a Ukrainian drone campaign that has isolated Crimea and reportedly hit about half of Russia's refining capacity. The piece contends Putin's main path to victory is to erode Western support for Kyiv, especially American, by exploiting President Trump's instinct to defer to him. It cites a sequence of concessions: a diesel purchase waiver, pressure on Ukraine to stop refinery strikes, waived sanctions, and a trilateral meeting with Xi. The authors warn that Russia now presses for NATO to return to its 1997 borders, which would expose Central and Eastern European members.
brief.argument: Putin is using a psychological operation aimed at Trump to win in Ukraine by securing American concessions that weaken Kyiv and expose NATO's eastern members.

title: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro outlines his vision for US leadership in the world
summary: At the Atlantic Council's NATO in America conference, Shapiro said the United States has an opportunity to push forward a new foreign policy centered on security and prosperity. The post Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro outlines his vision for US leadership in the world appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro outlined his vision for US global leadership at an Atlantic Council NATO conference.

brief.summary: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, speaking at the Atlantic Council's NATO in America conference, argues that after the 2026 midterms the US has a chance to build a new foreign policy that ties security to economic prosperity. He contends that the US forgot how inseparable its economy and security are, and that allied economic strength should sit alongside mutual defence as a core purpose of alliances. He proposes an allied investment platform that speeds up permitting and investment screening, along with tax incentives and preferential financing for allied projects. He also calls for coordinated international AI regulation, including third-party oversight of frontier models, to push China toward the same rules. He criticises Trump's tariffs and his handling of the Shenzhen meeting with Xi and Putin, and urges a firm NATO commitment and continued force posture in Europe. He lists early congressional priorities such as ending the Iran war, resuming aid to Ukraine, and sanctioning Russia.
brief.argument: The authors' central claim is that the US should fuse alliance security with shared economic strength, using allied investment and coordinated AI rules, instead of the tariff-driven approach the speaker attributes to Trump.
recommendations: Create an allied investment platform that fast-tracks permitting and investment screening for transatlantic industrial projects
Offer tax incentives and preferential financing for projects from allied countries
Build international consensus on AI regulation, including third-party oversight of frontier models

brief.summary: The piece is a book roundup from Al Majalla covering two Arabic-language titles. The first, by Palestinian historian Nazmi Jubeh, is an encyclopaedic study of Jerusalem under Mamluk rule, which the authors describe as a turning point. It argues that sultans, emirs, scholars, merchants and women shaped the city through religious patronage, endowments and construction, and that Jerusalem's architecture kept the broader Mamluk style while adding local features. Jubeh documents over 100 buildings and frames heritage protection as defending history and identity. The second title, by Hamid Dabashi (translated into Arabic), argues that the Gaza genocide has shaken Western claims to defend human rights. Dabashi questions whether the problem is double standards or lies in the foundations of Western civilisation, locating it in a long history of colonialism, imperialism and racial supremacy rather than in any single government.
brief.argument: Jerusalem's Mamluk-era architecture and institutions record the city's political and religious history, while Dabashi contends that the Gaza genocide reveals deeper flaws in Western civilisation's moral claims.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the 20 November EU-UK summit in Brussels, Andy Burnham's first with von der Leyen and Costa, followed the familiar pattern of European summits: deals were small and largely built on the May 2025 understanding under Starmer. The three agreements, on food and agriculture, carbon-emission trading alignment and a youth-experience scheme, are estimated by a Treasury assessment to add up to 0.5% to GDP, a fraction of Brexit's cost of 4% or more. Many implementation details remain unsettled, including UK influence over food standards, student tuition fees and access to the EU's "Made in Europe" rules. The piece shows the two sides linking the deals in bargaining, with each threatening that one could lapse if the other is not satisfied. It contrasts these minor details with Burnham's wider conversation on future relations, which is complicated by divisions within Labour and a domestic push against reversing Brexit. The authors judge that the reset may stall at electricity-market linkage, since the EU rejects cherry-picking its single market.
brief.argument: The EU-UK summit's deals are modest, unfinished and tied to bargaining, and the reset is unlikely to go far beyond electricity-market linkage because the EU refuses partial access to its single market.

title: When General William Westmoreland Said the “End Begins to Come Into View” in Vietnam
summary: Shielding the public from unpleasant truths about U.S. military operations abroad can backfire on a president.

brief.summary: The authors, through James M. Lindsay's essay, argue that General William Westmoreland's November 1967 National Press Club speech, given at President Johnson's request, gave an overly optimistic picture of the Vietnam War. They trace how the Americanization of the war failed to break the battlefield deadlock, how rising casualties and a shift in public opinion pressured Johnson, and how the administration chose to shore up support through favourable messaging rather than a clear change of course. The piece presents the Tet Offensive of January 1968 as exposing that rosy picture, contributing to Johnson's decision not to seek reelection. The lesson drawn is that shielding the public from unpleasant realities about overseas military operations can backfire on a president.
brief.argument: Westmoreland's overly upbeat 1967 public assessment of the Vietnam War, made to shore up political support, was discredited by the Tet Offensive and helped undermine Johnson's presidency.

summary: Shenzhen: a peace to end all peace? newspress_en Sat, 11/21/2026 - 18:35 Opinion The Shenzhen summit, which brought together the presidents of the United States, China and Russia, has drawn comparisons to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when American, Soviet and British leaders met to discuss the shape of the post-war world. What makes this summit different is that Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met before the guns had fallen silent, amid a race for influence,…

ai.sum: Trump, Xi and Putin held a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, drawing comparisons to Yalta.

brief.summary: The authors read the Shenzhen summit of Trump, Xi and Putin as a Yalta-style meeting held while wars in Iran and Ukraine were still active. Its declaration did not settle either war, but two of its four provisions bear on the Middle East without naming it: stable energy flows and nuclear non-proliferation. The authors argue that energy language looks economic but carries security stakes, because Iran can threaten Hormuz and its Houthi proxies can threaten Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea without fully closing either waterway; insurance costs and rerouted shipping are enough to damage the global economy. They note the three powers share an interest in stable supply but calculate differently: China depends heavily on Gulf crude, while the US remains exposed to global price rises despite its domestic output. The piece presents the summit as a sign of great-power bargaining over the region rather than a settlement.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen declaration's energy and nuclear provisions are security measures aimed at the Iran war and Red Sea shipping, even though they are framed in economic terms.

summary: After Shenzhen: the world just got more dangerous newspress_en Sat, 11/21/2026 - 16:03 Politics Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, in an extravagant spectacle of friendship. The historic trilateral meeting featured warm handshakes, tarmac hugs, and extended arms for the world's cameras. Beijing called the summit "groundbreaking"; Trump scored it "12 out of 10” and referred to both…

ai.sum: Xi hosted Trump and Putin at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen in a trilateral summit that commentators say makes the world more dangerous.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen summit between Xi, Trump and Putin, despite its warm staging, masked deep divisions over Ukraine, Iran and the emerging world order. They contend the three powers share a disdain for institutions that constrain them, such as the ICC, while keeping selective multilateralism for institutions that serve them, like the Security Council veto. On arms control, they read Xi's call to ban and destroy all nuclear weapons as a polite rejection of Trump's trilateral deal rather than a real concession. China's arsenal of roughly 600 warheads is far smaller than the US and Russian stockpiles, so proportional cuts would hit Beijing first and it would not accept them. Offering total disarmament costs China nothing and casts it as the principled party.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen summit's displays of cordiality concealed shared contempt for binding international institutions and a Chinese refusal to disarm in step with the US and Russia.
